clue.text: Obey guards united by lives changed by force

indicators.note: a word that guards something stands around it, so the other pieces go inside

parts.note: to obey an order is to comply with it

indicators.note: being united by something means being joined to it, so one piece sits directly beside the next

parts.note: U is the standard abbreviation for united, as in football club names

indicators.note: something changed has been altered, so the letters of the word before it are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written before being rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone who once obeyed rules finds their life has been transformed by coercion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guards' looks like soldiers, but it means the word for obey wraps around everything else, splitting four letters from the last two.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting compulsively means acting under an irresistible compulsion, an internal force one cannot resist.

clue.text: Local criminal regularly goes for artwork

indicators.note: something criminal is crooked or bent, so the letters of the word before it are twisted out of order

parts.note: taken as written before being rearranged

indicators.note: regularly means at fixed intervals, so every other letter of the next word is kept

parts.note: the first and third letters of goes

explanation.surface: A neighbourhood crook habitually turns to art, perhaps as a forger or vandal.
explanation.definitionFit: A collage is a work of art made by sticking pieces of paper, fabric and photos onto a backing.

clue.text: Sailor's fate depending on ship's officer

indicators.note: in a down clue, something depending on another hangs below it, so the second piece sits under the first

parts.note: a mate is a deck officer on a merchant ship
one's lot is one's fate in life

explanation.surface: A seaman's destiny rests on the whim of an officer aboard ship.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue names the lower piece first; in a down entry the piece that depends hangs beneath the officer.
explanation.definitionFit: Matelot is informal British slang, from French, for a sailor in the navy.

clue.text: Highlight one name in several foreign articles

indicators.note: the small word in places the preceding pieces inside the following one

parts.note: UN, DER and LE are the indefinite article in French and the definite articles in German and French
I is the Roman numeral one
N is the standard abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: An instruction to emphasise one name appearing in several foreign newspaper pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Articles' suggests newspaper pieces; here it means grammatical words like a and the, in French and German. I and N go inside LE, the last of them.
explanation.definitionFit: To underline something is to draw a line beneath it, and figuratively to stress or highlight it.

clue.text: Support for member of cast

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a strap that holds up an injured arm, a member being a limb
second meaning: to throw or hurl

explanation.surface: Backing given to one particular actor in a play's company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member of cast' reads as an actor; split it, and member means a limb and cast is a verb meaning throw.
explanation.definitionFit: A sling is both a bandage loop supporting an injured arm and, as a verb, to throw something carelessly.

clue.text: Very unfortunate time of life for Hamlet

parts.note: V is the standard abbreviation for very
ill as in ill luck or ill-starred
one's age is one's time of life

explanation.surface: Hamlet, the Prince of Denmark, has a wretched time at his point in life.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet looks like Shakespeare's prince; it is a small settlement here.
explanation.definitionFit: A hamlet is a small cluster of houses, a settlement smaller than or similar to a village.

clue.text: Green energy originally extracted from explosive fuel

indicators.note: something extracted from a word is pulled out of it, leaving the rest behind

parts.note: gelignite is a powerful blasting explosive

indicators.note: originally means at the start, so only the opening letter of each of those words is used

parts.note: first letters of green and energy

explanation.surface: Renewable power was first taken from volatile fuel.
explanation.walkthrough: GE comes off the front of GELIGNITE to leave the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Lignite is soft brown coal, burned as fuel especially in power stations.

clue.text: Current bishop upset believers incapable of rehabilitation?

parts.note: I is the symbol for electric current

indicators.note: upset means knocked over or disturbed, so the letters of the next word are thrown into a new order

parts.note: Right Reverend, abbreviated RR, is the formal title of a bishop
taken as written before being rearranged

explanation.surface: A present-day bishop angers his congregation, who now seem beyond redemption.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the definition is loose: something that cannot be reversed cannot be restored to its former state.
explanation.definitionFit: Irreversible means impossible to undo or restore, so such a thing can never be brought back or rehabilitated.

clue.text: Told story about wine bottles

indicators.note: to bottle something is to hold it inside, so the preceding piece sits within the word before

parts.note: red is wine of that colour

indicators.note: about can mean turned around, so the word before it is read from right to left

parts.note: a tale is a story

explanation.surface: Someone recounts an anecdote about wine being put in bottles.
explanation.walkthrough: The backwards story goes inside RED: R-ELAT-ED.
explanation.definitionFit: To relate a story is to tell it, so related is the past tense equivalent of told.

clue.text: This author will say almost everybody is wrong

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter of the following word is dropped

parts.note: the setter, this author, would say I'll for I will
eg, for example, is what say means when introducing an instance
everybody is all

explanation.surface: The setter declares that nearly everyone else is mistaken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This author will' is the setter speaking: I'LL, with the apostrophe ignored. ALL loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Something illegal is against the law, a legal and moral wrong.

clue.text: Sunny day warmed up around middle of afternoon

parts.note: day is daylight, as opposed to night

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so the preceding word wraps the piece that follows

parts.note: to heat something is to warm it up

indicators.note: the middle of a word is its central letter, the only one kept here

parts.note: the fifth of nine letters in afternoon

explanation.surface: A bright day that got warmer around mid-afternoon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sunny' looks like part of the weather report, but it is the definition, meaning cheerful.
explanation.definitionFit: A sunny disposition is cheerful, so sunny and lighthearted are synonyms describing a carefree mood.

clue.text: Learner failing to finish book bothered facilitator

indicators.note: bothered means disturbed or flustered, so the preceding letters are jumbled
failing to finish means stopping short, so the final letter of the word before is lost

parts.note: taken as written, before it loses its last letter
B is the standard abbreviation for book

explanation.surface: A student who didn't finish reading flustered the tutor helping them.
explanation.walkthrough: LEARNE plus B are mixed up together.
explanation.definitionFit: An enabler makes something possible, just as a facilitator eases a process along.

clue.text: Conspicuous-looking daggers

definitions.meaning: second meaning: staring angrily at someone

explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen joins two separate definitions into what reads as one phrase about obvious-looking knives.
explanation.definitionFit: Glaring is both an adjective for something blatantly obvious and a participle for staring fiercely and angrily.

clue.text: Choose course of graduate lectures

indicators.note: a course of something runs through it, so the letters run on within the following words

parts.note: spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Advice to pick which postgraduate lecture series to attend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Course of graduate lectures' reads as a university programme; it is where the letters lie: graduatE LECTures.
explanation.definitionFit: To elect is to choose, whether by voting or by deciding to do something.

clue.text: Step up to change side associated with undesirable elements

indicators.note: changing side swaps right for left, so one letter standing for a side is exchanged

parts.note: an increment is a step up, an increase

explanation.surface: Advice to raise one's game by switching away from unsavoury company.
explanation.walkthrough: The R (right) in INCREMENT becomes L (left). 'Undesirable elements' sounds like bad people; the elements are the weather.
explanation.definitionFit: Inclement weather is harsh and stormy, the kind of elements nobody wants to be out in.

clue.text: Snubbed couple getting put up by relative is a sore point

indicators.note: in a down clue, putting something up reads it from bottom to top
snubbed suggests a nose cut short, so the last letter of the word that follows is docked

parts.note: a brace is a pair, as of game birds
an uncle is a relative

explanation.surface: A couple ignored but taken in by family members find it a touchy subject.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A sore point' sounds like a touchy topic but is a literal sore on the skin.
explanation.definitionFit: A carbuncle is a severe boil or abscess on the skin, a painful inflamed spot.

clue.text: Relatively unimportant half?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: trivial, a matter of little consequence
second meaning, playfully: a half is a half-pint, so a modest measure of ale

explanation.walkthrough: In a British pub, a half is a half-pint glass of beer. The question mark flags the playful second reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Small beer is an idiom for trivial matters, and literally a half-pint is a small serving of ale.

clue.text: Great shot capturing Los Angeles as a whole

indicators.note: capturing means taking in, so the following piece is held inside
shot means ruined or wrecked, so the letters of the word before it are scattered

parts.note: taken as written before being rearranged
LA is the usual abbreviation for Los Angeles

explanation.surface: A fine photograph capturing the whole of Los Angeles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Great shot' reads as praise for a photo; shot is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: At large can mean in general or as a whole, as in the public at large.

clue.text: Take care of appearance away from home

parts.note: one's look is one's appearance
someone out is not at home

explanation.surface: Advice to tend one's appearance while travelling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take care of' reads as one phrase, but 'of' is only a link here.
explanation.definitionFit: Look out is an imperative warning meaning be careful, watch yourself.

clue.text: Generous bribe failing to retain All Blacks

indicators.note: failing to retain means letting slip, so a letter is lost from the word before

parts.note: to nobble is British slang for to bribe or tamper with someone
B stands for black, as on pencils; one of the two goes

explanation.surface: A generous bribe fails to keep the New Zealand rugby team on side.
explanation.walkthrough: The All Blacks are New Zealand's rugby team, but here the phrase only supplies a B for black to drop from NOBBLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Noble can mean magnanimous or high-minded, so a noble gesture is a generous one.

clue.text: Pet allowed to get small collar?

parts.note: to neck is to kiss and cuddle, as is to pet
let means allowed

explanation.surface: A household pet permitted to have a little collar.
explanation.walkthrough: Pet looks like an animal; it is the verb meaning to kiss and cuddle.
explanation.definitionFit: A necklet is a close-fitting ornament or fur worn round the neck, much like a small collar.

clue.text: Shortcut favoured by busy workers?

parts.note: surface reading: the quickest route used by hard-pressed employees
setter's reading: busy workers are worker bees, and the straight flight they take home

explanation.walkthrough: Bees are proverbially busy, and worker bees are the ones that forage, flying straight back to the hive.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the most direct route between two points, from the straight flight attributed to bees.

clue.text: What helps forge work of Nobel laureate?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the device that pumps air into a blacksmith's fire
second meaning: something by Saul Bellow, the American novelist who won the Nobel prize in 1976

explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning reads the answer as a possessive, Bellow's, as in a novel of his.
explanation.definitionFit: Bellows blow air to raise a smith's fire, and Bellow's names a work belonging to the Nobel-winning author.

clue.text: Author keeps first of his books here?

definitions.text: Author keeps first of his books here?

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so the following piece goes inside

parts.note: the author speaking of oneself, the writer's own self

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter, the only one kept

parts.note: opening letter of his

explanation.surface: A writer stores the first copies of their own books in a particular spot.
explanation.walkthrough: H goes inside SELF. Read whole, the clue also describes the place where an author keeps books, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A shelf is the flat board on which books are stored, so it is where an author would keep them.

clue.text: Ambiguous rule can get broken

indicators.note: something that gets broken falls to pieces, so the letters of the two words before are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written before being rearranged

explanation.surface: A vaguely worded regulation is easy to breach.
explanation.definitionFit: Something ambiguous is open to more than one interpretation and so not clear in meaning.

clue.text: Stud may enter this noble order of chivalry

parts.note: an earl is a nobleman
the OBE is the Order of the British Empire, a British honour

explanation.surface: A stallion at stud might be admitted to an aristocratic knightly order.
explanation.walkthrough: Stud suggests a breeding horse; it is an earring stud. The OBE, Officer of the Order of the British Empire, is a British honour.
explanation.definitionFit: A stud earring is pushed through a pierced hole in the soft lower lobe of the ear.

clue.text: Clash with dog chewing end of lead

indicators.note: a dog chewing something holds it in its mouth, so the piece goes inside

parts.note: a collie is a breed of sheepdog

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, which is the only one used

parts.note: last letter of lead

explanation.surface: An owner's fight with a dog that keeps chewing its lead.
explanation.definitionFit: To collide is to crash into, and figuratively to clash or come into conflict.

clue.text: C for Communist?

parts.note: surface reading: a political label, C standing for a party on the left
setter's reading: the letter C sits at the far left of the word centre

explanation.walkthrough: The political sense is the decoy; the question mark admits that communists are further left than this.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes moderate leftish politics and, literally, the position of the opening letter of the word centre.
